title: \'I don't want to die\': Police deploy stun gun on Blood Tribe member, tackle and punch him before he died, ASIRT says
subtitle: \'I was really sick to my stomach, because, you know, as Indigenous people, unfortunately, we are so used to reading how disposable our lives are,\' said Michelle Robinson, a member of the Sahtu Dene First Nation and activist
article: An unarmed man who died after an encounter with Calgary police in a hotel lobby last week repeatedly told officers he did not want to die before he was punched and Tased, Alberta\'s police watchdog said Wednesday.
And a defence lawyer said he\'s horrified by the apparent conduct of officers in the incident that was captured by police-worn body cameras.

Jon Wells died Sept. 17 following an altercation in which officers applied "various uses of force" inside the Carriage House Hotel, according to an Alberta Serious Incident Response Team (ASIRT) release.
As its investigation continues, the organization outlined the events it said ultimately led to the death of Wells, a 42-year-old Blood Tribe member.
The in-custody fatality unfolded after Calgary police were called to the Macleod Trail S.E. hotel shortly before 1 a.m. to help remove an unwanted person from the lobby, according to the release.
Wells - who had told officers, "I don\'t want to die" - would soon after be declared deceased on the hotel floor, his hands cuffed and legs restrained.
The ASIRT release, which does not identify Wells by name, said he had been tackled, punched and struck by stun guns before he died.

"I was really sick to my stomach, because, you know, as Indigenous people, unfortunately, we are so used to reading how disposable our lives are," said Michelle Robinson, a member of the Sahtu Dene First Nation, activist and podcast host.
"It\'s unacceptable, and so I\'m just heartbroken for the family reading this," she said. "This is a well-respected treaty member, and here he was treated this way, in the most horrendous way."
ASIRT said the first officer to arrive at the hotel found a man standing near the check-in desk.
"The male is standing with his hands in full view and does not possess any weapons," its release states.
He is ordered to leave the lobby but continued to stand in place, acting in a "confused" fashion, as he was seen attempting to pick up non-existent items off the floor.
The officer is then seen pointing a stun gun at the man and ordering him to leave the lobby following a 30-second conversation.
"The male raises his hands and confirms he\'ll leave and asks the officer not to shoot him," the release states.
"I don\'t want to die," he tells the officer while slowly walking toward the main door with his hands raised.

When two other officers enter through the main doors, Wells stops walking while repeating that he doesn\'t want to die. The first officer on scene then holstered his stun gun and attempted to grab the male.
"At no point during the interaction had the male been identified, nor was he ever told he was being detained or under arrest," ASIRT said.
Wells "physically resists" being grabbed before he\'s tackled by a second officer who then punches him in the head while both are on the ground, the release states.

It\'s at that time the first officer on scene, and a third, deployed their stun guns, also referred to as conducted energy weapons. Over the next 31⁄2 minutes, the three officers and Wells were involved in a physical altercation with "various uses of force resorted to by the officers."
Once on the floor, Wells was detained with handcuffs and leg restraints. He is "noted to be bleeding from the mouth and vomits."
A "spit mask" was then applied while he was lying face down on the floor.
Paramedics administered a sedative about seven minutes after Wells was handcuffed and still lying face down.

"The male is then left face down in handcuffs, leg restraints and a spit mask for about another three minutes until it is noted that he is unresponsive. The male was then provided medical care but declared deceased at the scene."
Robinson believes there is more to be done when police officers interact with Indigenous people.
"Their education isn\'t there. In fact, I would say their upbringing in society in general," Robinson said.
She believes police should be held accountable.
"It\'s not from a lack of solutions brought forward by the Indigenous community," she said. "We have multiple, multiple reports with so many recommendations, calls to action, calls to justice."
Part of ASIRT\'s mandate is to independently and objectively investigate incidents involving Alberta\'s police that have resulted in serious injury or death to any person.
"ASIRT\'s investigation will examine the use of force by the officers. No additional information will be released," it said.

The detail contained in ASIRT\'s press release is "exceptional" and might speak to the agency\'s desire it be treated transparently, "because this case looks really bad," said Tom Engel, chairman of the Criminal Trial Lawyers\' Association\'s policing committee.
The police use of violence, he said, seems extremely troubling, adding the use of a spit mask on someone vomiting is dangerous.
"Their job was to de-escalate and they escalated it," said Engel.
"Anyone who doesn\'t find this disturbing needs their head examined ... it\'s just tragic, (police conduct) is not getting any better."
Engel said it\'s time body-worn camera footage be released to the public, something done frequently and quickly by police in U.S. jurisdictions.
Doug King, a criminal justice professor at Mount Royal University, said from what he\'s heard of the incident, he didn\'t find the details terribly surprising.

"The trends that we see in terms of Indigenous peoples being more subject to police contact, Indigenous people being more victims of crime, involved in crime, young Indigenous women being going missing and things like that," King said.
Those trends, he said, have been working within the criminal justice system for probably 50 or 60 years.
"I wasn\'t surprised to see the trends sadly," said King.
He said there will be lots of people who suspect wrongdoing by police, but that will become known through ASIRT\'s investigation.

"This was an individual who was loved and loved people and had a reputation within the community, it makes his death harder to understand, but that\'s why we have to have an ASIRT investigation," King said.
"When anyone passes away in these kinds of circumstances, the hurt felt by the family and friends is profound."
Information about the incident was revealed by ASIRT the same day the Calgary Police Service released its race data analysis reports.
In an emailed statement to Postmedia, Calgary police said the officers involved in the Sept. 17 event are on a standard 30-day leave.
Regarding the ASIRT investigation, the police service said: "Independent oversight of policing is important to the trust the public places in us."
"Any time a person dies in the custody of police, there should be significant rigour around ensuring officers were acting within their lawful authority during that interaction."
The Calgary Police Service said it is fully co-operating with the investigation.
"We know there is a family and a community grieving this loss, and our thoughts are with them during this difficult time," it added.
Police Chief Mark Neufeld called the incident multi-layered and "a very complex situation" that shouldn\'t be judged until the ASIRT investigation is completed.
"No Calgarians should feel like the Calgary Police Service is hunting, that is definitely not the case ... it\'s not like police chose the location or chose the situation," he said.
"We welcome the oversight, we welcome the transparency ... but I would just ask Calgarians to suspend judgment."
Given the body cam footage, Neufeld said the investigation should be completed quickly.
